analysis.one_liner: Gives internet users the right to opt in or opt out of how companies collect and share their personal data.
analysis.headline: Introduced with no cosponsors, the bill sat in the Senate Commerce Committee without a markup or vote until the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The BROWSER Act would require broadband providers and websites or apps that collect personal data to tell users clearly what their privacy policies are. Companies would need your express permission before using or sharing sensitive information like your health data, financial records, precise location, or browsing history; for less sensitive data you could opt out. It would let the Federal Trade Commission enforce these rules, and it would bar companies from making service conditional on giving up your privacy rights. It would also preempt state privacy laws, replacing them with this single federal standard.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary internet users — essentially everyone who goes online. Anyone whose health information, financial data, precise location, or browsing history is currently collected and shared without meaningful consent would gain the right to say no, and to change their mind at any time at no cost. Parents of children under 13 would get explicit opt-in control over their kids' data.

how_it_helps.text: Providers must give clear, conspicuous notice of their privacy policies before sign-up, keep that notice persistently available, and give advance notice of material changes.

Companies must obtain express opt-in consent before using or sharing sensitive information, defined to include financial data, health information, children's data, Social Security numbers, precise geolocation, the content of communications, and web browsing and app-usage history.

Users must be offered a simple, easy-to-use, free mechanism to grant, deny, or withdraw consent at any time, available in languages other than English when the provider does business in that language, and the choice must take effect promptly and stay in effect.
Companies may not condition or refuse service on a user's agreement to waive privacy rights, and may not retaliate against users who refuse.
The bill applies its rules to broadband providers (overriding the common-carrier exemption in FTC law) and is enforceable by the FTC as an unfair or deceptive practice.

analysis.who_pays: Internet companies whose revenue depends on tracking users — advertising-driven platforms, data brokers, and broadband providers that monetize browsing history — would lose the ability to collect and share this data without consent. Industry would argue some cost shows up as less-personalized free services.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ad-driven tech platforms, data brokers, ISPs

drawbacks.text: The bill preempts all state privacy laws, meaning stronger state rules — such as California's — would be displaced by this single federal standard; if the federal rules were weaker than a state's, consumers in that state would lose protection they have today.
The bill also nullifies Communications Act privacy regulations covering these practices, except those about emergency services, wiping out any stricter sector-specific rules.
Non-sensitive data could still be used by default unless the user affirmatively opts out, so a large share of ordinary data collection would continue without affirmative consent.
Enforcement runs only through the FTC; consumers would have no direct right to sue under the bill and would depend on the agency's capacity and willingness to act.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consent rights are real and cover the most sensitive categories of personal data, which is a meaningful gain for internet users. The design has a genuine weakness, though: the federal preemption could have replaced stronger state privacy laws with this federal baseline, so the net gain would depend on whether the federal rules proved as strong as the state rules they replaced. The bill is consumer-protective in intent but not the strongest version of such a law.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee never took it up before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Marsha Blackburn introduced the bill on January 28, 2021, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
No senator signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action — no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that profit from collecting and sharing users' browsing history, location, and other personal data — advertising platforms, data brokers, and broadband providers — because no consent rules were enacted, and existing practices continued unchanged.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and no vote ever occurred, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would require consent before companies use, disclose, or access browsing history, precise location, and other personal data that fuels targeted advertising, cutting into a core revenue stream. Its value to consumers depends entirely on whether it passes.

ISPs would be brought under FTC privacy rules and would need consent to use or share customers' browsing and location data, ending a practice that had otherwise continued after sector rules were repealed in 2017.

industries.industry: Large tech platforms and edge services
industries.note: Platforms collecting sensitive user data would face opt-in consent requirements that constrain ad targeting, but the bill's preemption of state law would have capped stronger state rules and preempted Communications Act privacy regulations, giving the industry one uniform federal standard instead of a patchwork.

These services would face new consent mechanics and notice duties, and industry argued less data monetization would reduce ad-supported free offerings; users would weigh that cost against control over their own data.
